> **[case-study]**
> **Ashcroft Solar**
> 
> Ashcroft Solar installs solar panels on homes in country Y. It forecasts sales using four-period centred moving averages drawn from five years of quarterly data. These show steady underlying growth and a strong seasonal pattern, with installations peaking in spring and summer.
> 
> The government has just announced that the subsidy paid to homeowners for solar installation will end in 18 months. The sales director argues the existing forecasting method is reliable because it is built on real data. The operations director argues that past data cannot capture the effect of the subsidy ending, and that the judgement of experienced installers should be used instead.

Evaluate whether Ashcroft Solar should continue to rely on time series analysis rather than qualitative forecasting when planning for the next two years.
parts.solution_md:
Time series analysis uses past sales data to identify an underlying trend and seasonal variations in order to forecast future sales **[K]**. Ashcroft Solar has five years of quarterly data and uses four-period centred moving averages **[Ap]**. This smooths out the strong spring and summer peak and isolates the trend, letting Ashcroft Solar plan how many installers to employ in each quarter and how much stock to hold **[An]**. Because it rests on recorded installations rather than opinion, it is also free from the optimism or pessimism of individual managers, which makes it a defensible basis for committing to staffing levels **[An]**

However, time series analysis extrapolates from the past and assumes the future resembles it **[K]**. The ending of the subsidy in 18 months has no precedent within the five years of data **[Ap]**. It is likely to produce a surge of installations as homeowners rush to claim the subsidy before the deadline, followed by a sharp fall once it is withdrawn, and a moving average will predict neither **[An]**. Recruiting installers on the strength of the trend would leave Ashcroft Solar heavily overstaffed within two years, carrying wage costs against far lower demand **[An]**

Overall, the answer depends on the time horizon rather than on which method is better **[E]**. For the next twelve months the subsidy remains in place and the seasonal pattern still holds, so time series analysis stays the more reliable guide for quarter-by-quarter operational planning **[E]**. Beyond the deadline it becomes actively misleading, because it would project growth into a period when the main driver of demand has been removed **[E]**. The choice presented is therefore a false one; Ashcroft Solar should keep time series analysis for short-term planning and use qualitative judgement to estimate the size and timing of the surge and the drop, since the two methods answer different questions **[E]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Brackenfield**
> 
> Brackenfield produces bottled fruit drinks in country P. Research carried out two years ago estimated the price elasticity of demand for its main product at -1.8. The marketing director wants to cut the price by 10%, expecting sales volume to rise by 18%.
> 
> Since that research was completed, two new competitors have entered the market with similar drinks, a government health campaign has discouraged consumption of sugary drinks, and Brackenfield has launched a reformulated low-sugar version of the product. Its factory is currently operating at 88% capacity.

Evaluate whether Brackenfield should rely on its price elasticity of demand estimate of -1.8 when deciding to cut its price by 10%.
parts.solution_md:
Price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price **[K]**. Brackenfield's estimate of -1.8 was produced two years ago **[Ap]**. Since then two competitors have entered, a health campaign has discouraged sugary drinks, and the product itself has been reformulated, so the conditions under which -1.8 was measured no longer exist **[An]**. If the true elasticity is now weaker than 1, a 10% price cut would raise volume by less than 10% and total revenue would fall rather than rise, which is the opposite of what the marketing director expects **[An]**

A second problem is capacity **[K]**. The factory is already running at 88% **[Ap]**. Even if the estimate proves accurate and volume rises by 18%, Brackenfield could not produce the extra output without investment, so it would have surrendered margin on every unit sold while still failing to supply retailers who expected more stock **[An]**. Losing shelf space to the two new entrants at that point would be difficult to reverse, because retailers rarely restore listings quickly **[An]**

Overall, Brackenfield should not rely on the estimate as it stands **[E]**. The figure is not worthless; a bottled drink facing several substitutes is plausibly price elastic, so the direction is probably right, and that alone is useful **[E]**. What cannot be trusted is the precise value, and it is the precise value the 10% decision depends on, since the difference between an elasticity of 1.8 and one of 0.8 decides whether revenue rises or falls **[E]**. Brackenfield should re-estimate elasticity using current data, or trial the cut in one region first, and settle the capacity question before any national price change, because a correct forecast it cannot supply would still damage the business **[E]**

However, capacity could be raised with investment, so this is an argument about sequencing rather than a permanent barrier
> - Brackenfield could re-estimate elasticity from current data, or trial the cut in one region before committing nationally. However, both take time and money while competitors are already taking share, and price cuts are difficult to reverse because customers anchor to the lower price
>

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Loxley**
> 
> Loxley manufactures gardening tools in country E. Its sales have been flat for three years. The marketing director has suggested collecting ideas for new products from Loxley's own repair department, which sees which tools are returned as broken and how they have failed.

Explain **one** benefit to Loxley of using its repair department as a source of ideas for product development.
parts.solution_md:
Sources of ideas for product development include customers, employees, competitors and a business's own internal records **[1]**. Loxley's repair department sees at first hand which of its tools are returned as broken and the way in which they fail **[1]**. This gives Loxley evidence of specific design weaknesses that its own customers have actually experienced, so it can develop a more durable tool that solves a known problem rather than one based on guesswork, improving the chance that the new product sells and helping to lift sales that have been flat for three years **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Ideas for product development can come from customers, employees, competitors, research and development, or a business's own internal records
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The repair department sees which tools fail and how, giving evidence of real design weaknesses rather than assumptions
> - The information is already held inside Loxley, so it costs nothing extra to collect
> - Fixing a known fault addresses a problem customers have already met, making the improved product easier to market
> - Reducing the failure rate would also cut Loxley's repair and warranty costs, so the benefit is not limited to new sales
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Naming a source of ideas is the easy half; the marks come from saying what that source knows which others do not. A repair department is useful precisely because it sees failures that customers never bother to report and that sales figures cannot reveal. Whenever a question names a specific source, ask yourself what unique information sits there, and make that the centre of your answer.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Juniper Air**
> 
> Juniper Air is a budget airline operating in country V. It must decide six months in advance how many aircraft to lease for the summer season, and once signed, the leases cannot be cancelled.

Explain **one** reason why sales forecasting is important for Juniper Air.
parts.solution_md:
Sales forecasting is the process of estimating future sales, usually based on past data and expected market conditions **[1]**. Juniper Air must commit to leasing aircraft six months ahead of the summer season, and those leases cannot be cancelled once signed **[1]**. An accurate forecast allows it to lease the right number of aircraft, because leasing too many would mean paying fixed lease costs on planes flying with empty seats, while leasing too few would mean turning away passengers and losing revenue it could not recover later in the season **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Sales forecasting is the process of predicting future sales levels using past data and expected market conditions
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Aircraft leases must be signed six months ahead and cannot be cancelled, so the decision is irreversible and must be right first time
> - Leasing too many aircraft means paying fixed costs on planes carrying empty seats, reducing profit
> - Leasing too few means turning away passengers, and a summer season cannot be repeated once missed
> - Forecasts also allow Juniper Air to plan crew recruitment and training in line with the number of aircraft it will operate
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks why forecasting matters to a particular business, look for what that business cannot undo. Forecasting is far more valuable where a commitment is fixed and expensive than where a decision can be reversed cheaply. Here it is the uncancellable six-month lease that makes the forecast matter, so build your answer around that detail rather than around forecasting in general.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'promotional elasticity of demand'.
parts.solution_md:
Promotional elasticity of demand measures how responsive the quantity demanded of a product is to a change in spending on promotion **[1]**. It is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in promotional spending **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Promotional elasticity of demand is the responsiveness of demand for a product to a change in the amount spent promoting it, found by dividing the percentage change in quantity demanded by the percentage change in promotional spending
> - Promotional elasticity of demand shows by how much sales change when a business increases or reduces its promotional budget, expressed as a numerical value
> - Promotional elasticity of demand is a measure of how effective promotional spending is at generating additional sales of a product

> **[exam-tip]**
> Define the measure, not what its answer means. "Promotional elasticity tells you whether advertising is working" describes an interpretation and earns little; the definition needs to say what is being compared with what. Get the two percentage changes into your sentence first, and save the interpretation for questions that actually ask for it.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Portland Appliances**
> 
> Portland Appliances manufactures washing machines and refrigerators in country N. Its research shows the income elasticity of demand for its premium range is +2.4. Economists forecast that average incomes in country N will fall by 3% next year.

Explain **one** way in which the income elasticity of demand for its premium range may affect Portland Appliances' production decisions.
parts.solution_md:
Income elasticity of demand measures how responsive the quantity demanded of a product is to a change in consumer income **[1]**. Portland Appliances' premium range has an income elasticity of +2.4, which means it is a luxury good whose demand changes proportionally more than income does **[1]**. With incomes forecast to fall by 3%, demand for the premium range would be expected to fall by around 7.2%, so Portland Appliances should cut planned production of that range to avoid building up unsold stock and tying up cash in finished goods **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Income elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in consumer income
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A value of +2.4 identifies the premium range as a luxury good, so demand is highly sensitive to income changes
> - A 3% fall in income implies roughly a 7.2% fall in demand, allowing Portland Appliances to plan a specific reduction in output rather than guessing
> - Overproducing a luxury range in a downturn would leave unsold stock, tying up cash and storage space
> - Portland Appliances could shift capacity towards products with lower income elasticity, which would hold up better as incomes fall
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When you are given an elasticity value, direction and size are two separate pieces of information and the marks usually sit in the size. Saying demand will fall uses only the plus sign. Multiplying the elasticity by the income change, here 2.4 by 3%, turns a vague statement into a usable figure of about 7.2%, which is what lets you say something concrete about production.

Following the product development process is important for FF because launching metal frames represents a major step beyond its current capabilities **[K]**. Without this information, FF risks designing and producing frames that do not match what its target customers actually need, leading to the same rejection problems it currently experiences with plastic frames **[An]**

Prototype development and product testing are also important for FF in this context. Manufacturing metal frames requires different machinery, cutting techniques, and finishing processes to plastic **[K] [Ap]**. If FF attempts to move straight to full production without testing a prototype, it may discover serious manufacturing problems only after significant capital has been spent **[An]**. Given that FF is already considering other major investments, including 3D printers and entry into the retail market **[Ap]**, wasting resources on a poorly planned metal frame launch could seriously harm the business's financial position **[An]**

Overall, following the product development process is very important for FF, precisely because metal frames are so different from its current products **[Ap]** **[E]**. The process provides a structured way of managing the risk of entering unfamiliar territory. However, its value depends on FF's directors making a genuine commitment to fund the process properly - particularly market research and testing - and accepting that the process takes time before revenue is generated **[E]**. If the budget is inadequate or directors push for a faster launch, the process will be incomplete, and the risk of failure remains high regardless of whether the steps are followed **[E]**

parts.problem_md: Explain **one **way price elasticity of demand influences the pricing decisions of a business.
parts.solution_md:
Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how sensitive the quantity demanded of a product is to a change in its price **[1]**. If a business knows that demand for its product is price elastic, it can use this information to decide to lower its price, knowing that the percentage increase in the quantity demanded will be greater than the percentage fall in price  **[1]**. This means that total revenue will rise as a result of the price reduction  **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how much the quantity demanded of a product changes in response to a change in price
> - If demand is price elastic (PED > 1), a given percentage change in price leads to a larger percentage change in quantity demanded; if demand is price inelastic (PED < 1), the change in quantity demanded is smaller than the change in price
> 
> AO2
> 
> - If a business knows its product has price inelastic demand - for example, because it is unique or has few close substitutes - it can raise the price knowing that the percentage fall in demand will be smaller than the percentage increase in price. As a result, total revenue will increase, which suits a business whose objective is to maximise profit; this approach is commonly used by luxury goods brands or businesses with a strong USP that customers are reluctant to give up
> - A business can use PED to determine whether reducing prices is likely to increase total revenue; if a business knows demand for its product is price elastic, it can reduce the price and expect demand to rise by a greater percentage, increasing total revenue and potentially gaining market share from competitors. However, if the business misjudges PED and demand is actually inelastic, the price reduction will lead to lower total revenue, meaning the pricing decision backfires
> - The way in which PED influences pricing also depends on the business's objectives; a business that wants to maximise revenue will make different pricing decisions from one that wants to maximise market share - PED helps the business predict the likely outcome of each approach and choose the price that best meets its goals
> 
> Accept any other valid response

If demand for GG memberships is price inelastic, meaning members are not very sensitive to price, the fee increase will lead to only a small fall in the number of members, and GG's total revenue will rise **[1]**.
